passages.t: Jehoram walks in the ways of Ahab's house
passages.happening:
Jehoshaphat dies and his son Jehoram reigns (verse 1). Jehoshaphat had given his other sons silver, gold and fortified cities, but the kingdom to Jehoram as firstborn (verses 2-3). ‘When Jehoram had established himself over his father’s kingdom, he strengthened himself by putting to the sword all his brothers along with some of the princes of Israel’ (verse 4). ‘And Jehoram walked in the ways of the kings of Israel, just as the house of Ahab had done. For he married a daughter of Ahab and did evil in the sight of the LORD’ (verse 6).

‘Yet the LORD was unwilling to destroy the house of David, because of the covenant He had made with David, and since He had promised to maintain a lamp for David and his descendants forever’ (verse 7). Edom rebels and sets up its own king, and Libnah rebels too, ‘because Jehoram had forsaken the LORD, the God of his fathers’ (verse 10). He builds high places and leads Judah astray (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Jehoshaphat's marriage alliance with Ahab now bears its fruit. His son Jehoram, married to Ahab's daughter Athaliah, brings the religion and the violence of the northern royal house into Jerusalem. This is the darkest chapter so far. Jehoram reigned eight years, about 848 to 841 BC, probably after a time sharing the throne with his father. He is not the Jehoram, also called Joram, son of Ahab, who ruled the north at the same time; the two had the same name and were brothers-in-law.

A new king in the ancient world sometimes killed rival claimants, especially brothers given wealth and fortified cities, as Jehoshaphat's sons had been. Kings tells the revolt of Edom and Libnah; the killing of the brothers, Elijah's letter, the raid and the manner of Jehoram's death are only in Chronicles. Verse 2 calls Jehoshaphat king of Israel; the Chronicler often uses Israel for Judah, the faithful remnant carrying all Israel's identity.

Verse 7 holds out the thread of hope that runs through the book. A lamp, nir, kept burning in a house showed the family still lived there. As long as a son of David reigned, the lamp had not gone out. The promise will be tested almost to breaking in the next two chapters, when only one small child of David's line survives. The word prostitute, used three times in verses 11 to 13, is the prophets' picture of unfaithfulness to God as a marriage betrayed.
passages.later: Second Kings gives the same promise: ‘Yet for the sake of His servant David, the LORD was unwilling to destroy Judah, since He had promised to maintain a lamp for David and his descendants forever’ (2 Kings 8:19). Matthew's genealogy names him: ‘Jehoshaphat the father of Joram, and Joram the father of Uzziah’ (Matthew 1:8).
passages.asks: Jehoram secured his throne by killing his brothers, and still God kept the lamp burning for David's sake. Ask what you have tried to secure by harming someone in your way. And ask what it means to you that God's promise held even through the worst of David's sons.

passages.t: Elijah's letter, and a death no one regretted
passages.happening:
‘Then a letter came to Jehoram from Elijah the prophet’ (verse 12): because Jehoram has not walked in the ways of Jehoshaphat or Asa, but has led Judah into unfaithfulness like the house of Ahab and has killed his brothers, ‘who were better than you’ (verse 13), the LORD will strike his people, his sons, his wives and his possessions, and he himself will suffer a severe illness (verses 14-15).

The Philistines and Arabs invade, carry off the palace treasures and Jehoram's sons and wives, and only Jehoahaz, the youngest, is left (verses 16-17). ‘After all this, the LORD afflicted Jehoram with an incurable disease of the bowels’ (verse 18). After two years he dies, and his people make no fire in his honor (verse 19). ‘He died, to no one’s regret, and was buried in the City of David, but not in the tombs of the kings’ (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
The chapter reads as a reversal of Jehoshaphat's reign. Jehoshaphat was established because he sought God; Jehoram establishes himself by the sword. Elijah's letter follows the pattern of a prophet's judgment speech, charge and then sentence, and the narrative shows the sentence carried out. Prophets usually spoke in person, but letters were also used, as Jeremiah later wrote to the exiles. The youngest son, Jehoahaz, is called Ahaziah in the next chapter; both names mean the LORD has taken hold.

Burial honors mattered. The fire of spices given to Asa was withheld from Jehoram, and he was buried outside the royal tombs, a public disgrace. To no one's regret is one of the bleakest epitaphs in Scripture.

The text names Jehoram's illness as God's judgment on this one king, given by a prophet's word in advance. It is not a key for reading anyone else's illness.

It needs to be said plainly. The Bible does not teach that sickness comes from too little faith, or that a person who stays ill did not believe enough. Paul prayed and was not healed, and no one blames him. If you live with chronic illness, pain or disability, you are not a failure of faith. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.later: Second Kings tells the bare facts of his end: ‘And Jehoram rested with his fathers and was buried with them in the City of David’ (2 Kings 8:24).
passages.hard:
How could Elijah send a letter to Jehoram, when Elijah seems to have been taken up to heaven during Jehoshaphat's reign?

In 2 Kings 3, during a campaign in Jehoshaphat's lifetime, Elisha is the prophet consulted, which suggests that Elijah had already been taken up. Several explanations are offered. Some note that Jehoram probably reigned beside his father for some years before Jehoshaphat's death, and that the order of events in Kings is not strictly chronological, so Elijah may still have been active early in Jehoram's reign. Others suggest that Elijah wrote the letter before his departure, foreseeing Jehoram's conduct, and that it was delivered later. Some critical scholars think the Chronicler gave the prophecy to Elijah as the great prophet of the struggle against Ahab's house, without meaning a precise claim about dates. The chronology of this period is complex, and the question remains open.
passages.asks: Jehoram died to no one's regret. Ask what people will say of the way you used your power over them. And ask whose good name in your family you are living on, or spending.
